title: Optional Mathematics: Unit-wise Subjective Question Bank
html:
Group A is ten single marks. The other 40 marks of the Optional Mathematics paper come from Group B (ten 2-mark questions) and Group C (five 4-mark questions), and here marks are won by method, not by recall.

A 2-mark answer needs two visible steps; a 4-mark answer needs a figure or a table where one helps, the formula, the substitution, the working and a checked answer.

This chapter takes the ten units of the Optional Mathematics 8 book in order. Each unit opens with a model question worked the way a marker wants to see it, followed by four 2-mark and three 4-mark questions with complete solutions.

How to use this bank

Read the model question first. Then cover the solutions and write the seven questions out in full, on paper, against the clock: about 4 minutes for a 2-mark question and 10 minutes for a 4-mark question.

Mark yourself step by step, not just by the final answer. In the real paper a correct method with one arithmetic slip still earns most of the marks, while a bare answer with no working may earn none.

Practice items, not past questions

Every question below is an original practice item written for the 50-mark school paper and the chapters of the Optional Mathematics 8 book. None is claimed to have appeared in any school's paper.

All numerical answers were worked out independently, and most solutions end with the check that proves them.

21.1 Relation and Function

Model question: a function and its inverse relation

Problem. Let A=\{1,2,3,4\}, B=\{2,4,6,8,10\} and f: A\rightarrow B be defined by f(x)=2x. (i) Write f as a set of ordered pairs and show it in an arrow diagram. (ii) Write its domain, co-domain and range.

(iii) Write the inverse relation f^{-1}. Is f^{-1} a function from B to A? Give a reason.

Solution. (i) f(1)=2, f(2)=4, f(3)=6, f(4)=8, so f=\{(1,2),(2,4),(3,6),(4,8)\}. In the arrow diagram, 1, 2, 3, 4 in the first oval send one arrow each to 2, 4, 6, 8; the member 10 of B receives no arrow.

(ii) Domain =A=\{1,2,3,4\}; co-domain =B=\{2,4,6,8,10\}; range =\{2,4,6,8\}.

(iii) f^{-1}=\{(2,1),(4,2),(6,3),(8,4)\}. As a relation from B to A it is not a function, because the member 10 of B has no image. (It would be a function from the range \{2,4,6,8\} to A.)

Check. Every member of A has exactly one image, so f itself is a function ✓.

  1. Find x and y if \left(\frac{x}{2}+1,\ y-2\right)=(3,\ x). [2]
  2. If P=\{a,b,c\} and Q=\{0,1\}, find Q\times P and n(P\times Q). [2]
  3. On A=\{1,2,3,6\}, list the relation R=\{(x,y): x \text{ is a factor of } y \text{ and } x\neq y\} and write its domain and range. [2]
  4. If f(x)=x^2-4x+3, find the pre-images of 0 and of 3. [2]
  5. A function f from A=\{-1,0,1,2\} to B=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\} is defined by f(x)=x^2+1. (i) Write f as ordered pairs. (ii) Find the range. (iii) Draw the arrow diagram. (iv) Is f one-to-one? Give a reason. [4]
  6. A function is defined by f(x)=ax+b. If f(2)=7 and f(-1)=-2, find a and b, then find f(5) and the pre-image of 19. [4]
  7. State, with reasons, which of these are functions: R_1=\{(1,1),(2,4),(3,9)\}; R_2=\{(4,2),(4,-2),(9,3)\}; R_3=\{(x,y): y=3\} on \{1,2,3\}; the circle x^2+y^2=4. Use the vertical line test where it helps. [4]
Solutions to 21.1

1. First components: \frac{x}{2}+1=3, so x=4. Second components: y-2=x=4, so y=6.

2. Q\times P=\{(0,a),(0,b),(0,c),(1,a),(1,b),(1,c)\} and n(P\times Q)=3\times2=6.

3. R=\{(1,2),(1,3),(1,6),(2,6),(3,6)\}. Domain =\{1,2,3\}; range =\{2,3,6\}.

4. Pre-images of 0: x^2-4x+3=0, (x-1)(x-3)=0, so x=1 or 3. Pre-images of 3: x^2-4x=0, x(x-4)=0, so x=0 or 4.

5. (i) f=\{(-1,2),(0,1),(1,2),(2,5)\}. (ii) Range =\{1,2,5\}. (iii) Arrows -1\rightarrow2, 0\rightarrow1, 1\rightarrow2, 2\rightarrow5; the members 0, 3 and 4 of B receive none. (iv) It is not one-to-one, because -1 and 1 have the same image 2. It is still a function (many-to-one).

6. 2a+b=7 and -a+b=-2. Subtracting, 3a=9, so a=3 and b=1: f(x)=3x+1. Then f(5)=16, and 3x+1=19 gives the pre-image x=6. Check: f(2)=7 ✓, f(-1)=-2 ✓.

7. R_1: a function, each first component appears once. R_2: not a function, 4 has two images, 2 and -2. R_3=\{(1,3),(2,3),(3,3)\}: a function (constant), each input has the one image 3. The circle: not a function, the vertical line x=0 meets it at (0,2) and (0,-2).

21.2 Polynomials

Model question: sum, difference and product

Problem. If f(x)=2x^3-x+3 and g(x)=x^2-2x+1, find f(x)+g(x), f(x)-g(x) and f(x)\cdot g(x). State the degree of each result and check the product at x=2.

Solution.

f+g=2x^3+x^2-3x+4 \quad(\text{degree }3),\qquad f-g=2x^3-x^2+x+2 \quad(\text{degree }3)

For the product, multiply each term of f by each term of g:

(2x^3-x+3)(x^2-2x+1)=2x^5-4x^4+2x^3-x^3+2x^2-x+3x^2-6x+3

=2x^5-4x^4+x^3+5x^2-7x+3 \quad(\text{degree }3+2=5)

Check at x=2. f(2)=16-2+3=17 and g(2)=4-4+1=1, so f(2)g(2)=17. The product gives 64-64+8+20-14+3=17 ✓.

  1. Write the degree, the leading coefficient and the constant term of 3x^2-5+2x^4-x. [2]
  2. Find a and b if (a-1)x^2+2x+3=4x^2+(b+1)x+3. [2]
  3. Subtract 2x^3-3x^2+4 from x^3+x^2-2x+1. [2]
  4. Multiply (x+2)(x^2-3x+1). [2]
  5. If p(x)=x^3+2x^2-x, q(x)=2x^2-3x+4 and r(x)=x^3-5, find p(x)-q(x)+r(x) and its value at x=-1. [4]
  6. Find the product (2x^2-x+3)(x^2+2x-1), state its degree, and check it at x=1. [4]
  7. A rectangle is (3x-1) cm long and (x+4) cm wide. (i) Find its area. (ii) Find its perimeter. (iii) Find both when x=5, and check with the actual sides. [4]
Solutions to 21.2

1. In standard form 2x^4+3x^2-x-5: degree 4, leading coefficient 2, constant term -5.

2. x^2: a-1=4, so a=5. x: 2=b+1, so b=1.

3. (x^3+x^2-2x+1)-(2x^3-3x^2+4)=-x^3+4x^2-2x-3.

4. x^3-3x^2+x+2x^2-6x+2=x^3-x^2-5x+2.

5. x^3+2x^2-x-2x^2+3x-4+x^3-5=2x^3+2x-9. At x=-1: -2-2-9=-13. Check: p(-1)=2, q(-1)=9, r(-1)=-6, and 2-9-6=-13 ✓.

6. 2x^4+4x^3-2x^2-x^3-2x^2+x+3x^2+6x-3=2x^4+3x^3-x^2+7x-3; degree 4. At x=1: (2-1+3)(1+2-1)=4\times2=8, and 2+3-1+7-3=8 ✓.

7. (i) (3x-1)(x+4)=3x^2+11x-4 cm². (ii) 2[(3x-1)+(x+4)]=8x+6 cm. (iii) At x=5: area =75+55-4=126 cm², perimeter =46 cm. The sides are 14 cm and 9 cm: 14\times9=126 ✓ and 2(14+9)=46 ✓.

21.3 Sequence and Series

Model question: from terms to a sum

Problem. The first four terms of a sequence are 4, 9, 16, 25. (i) Find the general term. (ii) Find the 12th term. (iii) Is 225 a term? If so, which one? (iv) Write the sum of the first five terms in sigma notation and find it.

Solution. (i) The terms are 2^2, 3^2, 4^2, 5^2, so t_n=(n+1)^2.

(ii) t_{12}=13^2=169.

(iii) (n+1)^2=225=15^2 gives n+1=15, so n=14: 225 is the 14th term.

(iv) \sum_{k=1}^{5}(k+1)^2=4+9+16+25+36=90.

Check. t_1=(1+1)^2=4 ✓ and t_4=25 ✓.

  1. Write the first four terms of the sequence with t_n=\frac{2n-1}{n+1}. [2]
  2. Find the general term and the 15th term of 2, 6, 10, 14, \ldots. [2]
  3. Is 101 a term of 5, 9, 13, \ldots? If so, which term? [2]
  4. Find the value of \sum_{r=1}^{5}(r^2+1). [2]
  5. Triangles in a row are made of matchsticks: 1 triangle needs 3 sticks, 2 triangles 5 sticks, 3 triangles 7 sticks. (i) Find the general term. (ii) How many sticks make 20 triangles? (iii) How many triangles can be made with 61 sticks? (iv) Write the total sticks for the first five patterns in sigma notation and find it. [4]
  6. Find the general term of 0, 3, 8, 15, 24, \ldots by the method of differences, find the 10th term, and evaluate the sum of the first four terms written in sigma notation. [4]
  7. Using \sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}, find (i) \sum_{k=1}^{30}k (ii) \sum_{k=1}^{12}(2k+3) (iii) the sum of all the multiples of 4 from 4 to 100. [4]
Solutions to 21.3

1. t_1=\frac{1}{2}, t_2=\frac{3}{3}=1, t_3=\frac{5}{4}, t_4=\frac{7}{5}.

2. The difference is 4 and each term is 2 less than 4n: t_n=4n-2, so t_{15}=58.

3. t_n=4n+1. Setting 4n+1=101 gives n=25, a natural number, so 101 is the 25th term.

4. 2+5+10+17+26=60.

5. (i) The difference is 2 and each term is 1 more than 2n: t_n=2n+1. (ii) t_{20}=41 sticks. (iii) 2n+1=61 gives n=30 triangles. (iv) \sum_{k=1}^{5}(2k+1)=3+5+7+9+11=35 sticks.

6. First differences 3, 5, 7, 9; second differences 2, so compare with n^2: the terms are each 1 less, so t_n=n^2-1. Then t_{10}=99, and \sum_{k=1}^{4}(k^2-1)=0+3+8+15=26.

7. (i) \frac{30\times31}{2}=465. (ii) 2\sum_{k=1}^{12}k+\sum_{k=1}^{12}3=2\times78+36=192. (iii) 4+8+\cdots+100=4(1+2+\cdots+25)=4\times\frac{25\times26}{2}=4\times325=1300.

21.4 Limit

Model question: value and limit

Problem. Let f(x)=\frac{x^2+x-6}{x-2}. (i) Show that f(2) is not defined. (ii) Find f(x) for x=1.9, 1.99, 2.01 and 2.1. (iii) Find \lim_{x\to2}f(x) by factorising. (iv) Describe the graph of f.

Solution. (i) f(2)=\frac{4+2-6}{0}=\frac{0}{0}, which has no value.

(ii) f(1.9)=4.9, f(1.99)=4.99, f(2.01)=5.01, f(2.1)=5.1.

(iii) x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2), so for x\neq2, f(x)=x+3 and \lim_{x\to2}f(x)=2+3=5.

(iv) The graph is the straight line y=x+3 with a hole at the point (2,5).

Check. The table approaches 5 from both sides, as the algebra says ✓.

  1. Write the next three terms of \frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{6}, \ldots and state the limit of the sequence. [2]
  2. Evaluate \lim_{x\to-2}(3x^2-x+1). [2]
  3. Evaluate \lim_{x\to5}\frac{x^2-25}{x-5}. [2]
  4. Evaluate \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{4n-1}{n}. [2]
  5. Evaluate (i) \lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-5x+6}{x-3} (ii) \lim_{x\to-1}\frac{x^2-1}{x+1} (iii) \lim_{x\to4}\frac{x^2-3x-4}{x-4}. [4]
  6. After n steps of "shade half of what is left", the shaded fraction of a square is 1-\frac{1}{2^n}. (i) Write the first five values. (ii) State the limit. (iii) Find the least n for which the unshaded part is less than 0.001. [4]
  7. A function is defined by f(x)=2x+1 for x<2 and f(x)=7-x for x\geq2. (i) Find f(2). (ii) Find what f(x) approaches as x\rightarrow2^- and as x\rightarrow2^+. (iii) Does \lim_{x\to2}f(x) exist, and does it equal f(2)? [4]
Solutions to 21.4

1. The nth term is \frac{n}{n+2}, so the next terms are \frac{5}{7}, \frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4}, \frac{7}{9}. Since \frac{n}{n+2}=1-\frac{2}{n+2} and \frac{2}{n+2}\rightarrow0, the limit is 1.

2. Substitute: 3(4)+2+1=15.

3. \frac{(x-5)(x+5)}{x-5}=x+5\rightarrow10.

4. \frac{4n-1}{n}=4-\frac{1}{n}\rightarrow4.

5. (i) \frac{(x-2)(x-3)}{x-3}=x-2\rightarrow1. (ii) \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x+1}=x-1\rightarrow-2. (iii) \frac{(x-4)(x+1)}{x-4}=x+1\rightarrow5.

6. (i) \frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{4}, \frac{7}{8}, \frac{15}{16}, \frac{31}{32}. (ii) The unshaded part \frac{1}{2^n}\rightarrow0, so the limit is 1. (iii) \frac{1}{2^n}<\frac{1}{1000} needs 2^n>1000; 2^9=512 is too small and 2^{10}=1024 works, so n=10.

7. (i) x=2 uses the second rule: f(2)=7-2=5. (ii) From the left, 2x+1\rightarrow2(2)+1=5; from the right, 7-x\rightarrow5. (iii) Both sides approach 5, so the limit exists and equals 5, which is also f(2): the graph has no break at x=2.

21.5 Matrix

Model question: combining matrices

Problem. Let A=[(2,-1),(0,3)], B=[(1,4),(-2,5)] and C=[(3,0),(1,-1)]. Find (i) A+B-C (ii) 2A-3B (iii) the matrix X such that A+X=2B.

Solution. (i) A+B=[(3,3),(-2,8)], so A+B-C=[(3-3,\ 3-0),(-2-1,\ 8+1)]=[(0,3),(-3,9)].

(ii) 2A=[(4,-2),(0,6)] and 3B=[(3,12),(-6,15)], so 2A-3B=[(1,-14),(6,-9)].

(iii) X=2B-A=[(2,8),(-4,10)]-[(2,-1),(0,3)]=[(0,9),(-4,7)].

Check (iii). A+X=[(2+0,\ -1+9),(0-4,\ 3+7)]=[(2,8),(-4,10)]=2B ✓.

  1. Construct the 3\times2 matrix A=[a_{ij}] with a_{ij}=i-2j. [2]
  2. Find x, y and z if [(x+y,\ 2),(z,\ x-y)]=[(6,\ 2),(5,\ 2)]. [2]
  3. If [(a,\ 2b),(4,\ 1)] is symmetric and a+b=5, find a and b. [2]
  4. If A=[(3,-2),(1,4)], find 3A-2I, where I is the unit matrix of order 2. [2]
  5. If A=[(1,-2),(3,0)] and B=[(2,1),(-1,4)], verify that 3(A+B)=3A+3B. [4]
  6. Find the matrices X and Y if X+Y=[(5,2),(0,9)] and X-Y=[(3,6),(4,-1)]. [4]
  7. The marks of two students in three subjects are F=[(65,72,80),(58,66,75)] in the first term and S=[(70,68,85),(64,70,79)] in the second term (rows: students; columns: subjects). Find (i) the total marks F+S (ii) the change S-F, explaining any negative entry (iii) the average marks \frac{1}{2}(F+S). [4]
Solutions to 21.5

1. a_{11}=-1, a_{12}=-3, a_{21}=0, a_{22}=-2, a_{31}=1, a_{32}=-1, so A=[(-1,-3),(0,-2),(1,-1)].

2. z=5; x+y=6 and x-y=2 give x=4, y=2.

3. Symmetric means a_{12}=a_{21}: 2b=4, so b=2 and a=3.

4. 3A=[(9,-6),(3,12)] and 2I=[(2,0),(0,2)], so 3A-2I=[(7,-6),(3,10)].

5. A+B=[(3,-1),(2,4)], so 3(A+B)=[(9,-3),(6,12)]. 3A=[(3,-6),(9,0)] and 3B=[(6,3),(-3,12)], so 3A+3B=[(9,-3),(6,12)]. The two are equal.

6. Adding the equations, 2X=[(8,8),(4,8)], so X=[(4,4),(2,4)]. Then Y=[(5,2),(0,9)]-X=[(1,-2),(-2,5)]. Check: X-Y=[(3,6),(4,-1)] ✓.

7. (i) F+S=[(135,140,165),(122,136,154)]. (ii) S-F=[(5,-4,5),(6,4,4)]: the first student scored 4 marks fewer in the second subject; every other mark rose. (iii) \frac{1}{2}(F+S)=[(67.5,70,82.5),(61,68,77)].

21.6 Coordinate Geometry

Model question: an isosceles right-angled triangle

Problem. The vertices of a triangle are A(1,1), B(5,4) and C(-2,5). (i) Show that it is an isosceles right-angled triangle. (ii) Find its area. (iii) Find the mid-point of its hypotenuse.

Solution. (i) AB^2=4^2+3^2=25, AC^2=(-3)^2+4^2=25, BC^2=(-7)^2+1^2=50. So AB=AC=5 (isosceles) and AB^2+AC^2=50=BC^2, so the angle at A is a right angle.

(ii) Area =\frac{1}{2}\times AB\times AC=\frac{1}{2}\times5\times5=12.5 square units.

(iii) The hypotenuse is BC; its mid-point is \left(\frac{5-2}{2},\frac{4+5}{2}\right)=(1.5,\ 4.5).

Check (ii). \frac{1}{2}\left|1(4-5)+5(5-1)+(-2)(1-4)\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|-1+20+6\right|=12.5 ✓.

  1. Find the distance between (-3,-2) and (3,6). [2]
  2. Find the point that divides the join of (-4,6) and (8,-3) internally in the ratio 1:2. [2]
  3. Find the slope and the y-intercept of 3x+5y=15. [2]
  4. Find the equation of the line of slope -1 through (2,5). [2]
  5. Find k if (1,2), (3,k) and (6,12) are collinear, (i) using slopes (ii) using area. [4]
  6. Find the points that divide the join of A(-3,-1) and B(9,7) into four equal parts. [4]
  7. Show that P(-2,1), Q(3,-1), R(5,4) and S(0,6) are the vertices of a square, and find its area in two ways. [4]
Solutions to 21.6

1. \sqrt{6^2+8^2}=\sqrt{100}=10 units.

2. \left(\frac{1(8)+2(-4)}{3},\ \frac{1(-3)+2(6)}{3}\right)=(0,3).

3. 5y=-3x+15, so y=-\frac{3}{5}x+3: slope -\frac{3}{5}, y-intercept 3.

4. y=-x+c through (2,5): 5=-2+c, so c=7 and the line is y=-x+7.

5. (i) The slope from (1,2) to (6,12) is \frac{10}{5}=2, so the slope from (1,2) to (3,k) must be 2: \frac{k-2}{2}=2, k=6. (ii) \frac{1}{2}\left|1(k-12)+3(12-2)+6(2-k)\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|30-5k\right|=0 gives k=6 ✓.

6. The quarter points divide AB in the ratios 1:3, 1:1 and 3:1: \left(\frac{9-9}{4},\frac{7-3}{4}\right)=(0,1); the mid-point (3,3); \left(\frac{27-3}{4},\frac{21-1}{4}\right)=(6,5).

7. PQ^2=25+4=29, QR^2=4+25=29, RS^2=25+4=29, SP^2=4+25=29: all sides equal. Diagonals: PR^2=49+9=58 and QS^2=9+49=58: equal. Four equal sides and equal diagonals make a square. Area (i) = side^2=29 square units. (ii) Arrow method: (-2)(-1)-3(1)=-1; 3(4)-5(-1)=17; 5(6)-0(4)=30; 0(1)-(-2)(6)=12; total 58, so the area is \frac{58}{2}=29 ✓.

21.7 Trigonometry

Model question: a tree broken by the wind

Problem. A tree is broken by a storm at a point 6 m above the ground. Its top touches the ground, and the broken part makes an angle of 30^\circ with the ground.

Draw a figure and find (i) the length of the broken part (ii) the original height of the tree (iii) the distance from the foot of the tree to the point where the top touches the ground.

Solution. Figure. A vertical segment AB=6 m (the standing part), the broken part BC reaching the ground at C, and the right angle at A; the angle at C is 30^\circ.

(i) \sin30^\circ=\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{6}{BC}, so BC=\frac{6}{\frac{1}{2}}=12 m.

(ii) Original height =AB+BC=6+12=18 m.

(iii) \tan30^\circ=\frac{6}{AC}, so AC=6\sqrt{3}\approx10.39 m.

Check. AC^2+AB^2=108+36=144=12^2=BC^2 ✓.

  1. Convert 48^\circ36' into grades. [2]
  2. Express \left(\frac{7\pi}{10}\right)^c in degrees and in grades. [2]
  3. If \cos\theta=\frac{12}{13} and \theta is acute, find \tan\theta and \mathrm{cosec}\,\theta. [2]
  4. Find the value of \sin^245^\circ+\cos^230^\circ-\tan^260^\circ. [2]
  5. Prove that (i) (1+\tan^2\theta)(1-\sin^2\theta)=1 (ii) \sec\theta-\cos\theta=\sin\theta\tan\theta. [4]
  6. Find the values of (i) \sin240^\circ (ii) \cos150^\circ (iii) \tan(-45^\circ) (iv) \sin(90^\circ+30^\circ)+\cos(180^\circ-60^\circ). [4]
  7. From the top of a tower 30 m high, the angle of depression of a car on the road is 60^\circ. Draw a figure and find (i) the distance of the car from the foot of the tower (ii) the distance from the top of the tower to the car. [4]
Solutions to 21.7

1. 36'=\frac{36}{60}=0.6^\circ, so the angle is 48.6^\circ, and 48.6\times\frac{10}{9}=54^g.

2. \frac{7\times180^\circ}{10}=126^\circ and \frac{7\times200^g}{10}=140^g.

3. b=12, h=13, so p=\sqrt{169-144}=5. \tan\theta=\frac{5}{12} and \mathrm{cosec}\,\theta=\frac{13}{5}.

4. \frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{4}-3=\frac{2+3-12}{4}=-\frac{7}{4}.

5. (i) LHS =\sec^2\theta\cdot\cos^2\theta=\frac{1}{\cos^2\theta}\cdot\cos^2\theta=1= RHS. (ii) LHS =\frac{1}{\cos\theta}-\cos\theta=\frac{1-\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}=\sin\theta\cdot\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta= RHS.

6. (i) \sin(180^\circ+60^\circ)=-\sin60^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. (ii) \cos(180^\circ-30^\circ)=-\cos30^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}. (iii) -\tan45^\circ=-1. (iv) \cos30^\circ-\cos60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}.

7. Figure: the tower AB=30 m with the horizontal through the top A, the car C on the ground, and the 60^\circ depression at A equal to the elevation at C. (i) \tan60^\circ=\frac{30}{BC}, so BC=\frac{30}{\sqrt{3}}=10\sqrt{3}\approx17.32 m. (ii) \sin60^\circ=\frac{30}{AC}, so AC=\frac{60}{\sqrt{3}}=20\sqrt{3}\approx34.64 m.

21.8 Vector

Model question: a triangle described by vectors

Problem. The points are P(1,2), Q(4,6) and R(8,3). (i) Find \overrightarrow{PQ} and \overrightarrow{QR} and their magnitudes. (ii) What kind of triangle is PQR?

(iii) Verify that \overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{PR} and find |\overrightarrow{PR}|.

Solution. (i) \overrightarrow{PQ}=\binom{3}{4} with |\overrightarrow{PQ}|=5; \overrightarrow{QR}=\binom{4}{-3} with |\overrightarrow{QR}|=5.

(ii) Two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.

(iii) \overrightarrow{PR}=\binom{8-1}{3-2}=\binom{7}{1} and \overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\binom{3+4}{4-3}=\binom{7}{1} ✓. |\overrightarrow{PR}|=\sqrt{49+1}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}.

Check. 5^2+5^2=50=|\overrightarrow{PR}|^2, so the triangle is also right-angled at Q.

21.9 Transformation

Model question: one transformation after another

Problem. The triangle A(1,2), B(3,1), C(2,4) is reflected in the x-axis to A'B'C', and A'B'C' is rotated through +90^\circ about the origin to A''B''C''.

Find both images and describe what happens to the coordinates of a general point.

Solution. Reflection in the x-axis, (x,y)\rightarrow(x,-y): A'(1,-2), B'(3,-1), C'(2,-4).

Rotation +90^\circ, (x,y)\rightarrow(-y,x): A''(2,1), B''(1,3), C''(4,2).

A general point goes (x,y)\rightarrow(x,-y)\rightarrow(y,x): the two transformations together simply swap the coordinates. (This single transformation is the reflection in the line y=x, which you will meet in grade 9.)

Check. AB=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt{5} and A''B''=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt{5}: lengths are kept, as two isometric steps must keep them ✓.

The three habits that save marks

Write the formula before the numbers. Show the table in statistics and the figure in height and distance, because those are where method marks live.

And finish with a check, by substitution, by a second method, or by asking whether the answer is sensible: a tree 18 m tall is believable; one 180 m tall is not.

Extended questions

Model answer D1: matrix operations (10 marks)

Introduction. A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns. Matrices of the same order are added or subtracted by working on corresponding elements.

Two matrices are multiplied by taking each row of the first with each column of the second. Both given matrices are of order 2\times 2.

Addition. A + B = \begin{pmatrix}2+1&3+0\\1+2&4+5\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&9\end{pmatrix}.

Subtraction. B - A = \begin{pmatrix}1-2&0-3\\2-1&5-4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&-3\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.

Product AB. Row 1 of A with column 1 of B: 2(1) + 3(2) = 8. Row 1 with column 2: 2(0) + 3(5) = 15. Row 2 with column 1: 1(1) + 4(2) = 9. Row 2 with column 2: 1(0) + 4(5) = 20.

AB = \begin{pmatrix}8&15\\9&20\end{pmatrix}.

Product BA. Row 1 of B with column 1 of A: 1(2) + 0(1) = 2. Row 1 with column 2: 1(3) + 0(4) = 3. Row 2 with column 1: 2(2) + 5(1) = 9. Row 2 with column 2: 2(3) + 5(4) = 26.

BA = \begin{pmatrix}2&3\\9&26\end{pmatrix}.

Comparison. Since \begin{pmatrix}8&15\\9&20\end{pmatrix} \ne \begin{pmatrix}2&3\\9&26\end{pmatrix}, we have AB \ne BA.

Operation Result Rule
A + B (3 3; 3 9) add matching elements
B − A (−1 −3; 1 1) subtract matching elements
AB (8 15; 9 20) row × column
BA (2 3; 9 26) row × column

Conclusion. Addition of matrices is commutative, but multiplication is not, so the order of the factors must always be kept.

Model answer D2: coordinate geometry of a triangle (10 marks)

Introduction. For points (x_1, y_1) and (x_2, y_2) the distance is d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}, the midpoint is \left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right) and the point dividing in the ratio m:n is \left(\frac{mx_2+nx_1}{m+n}, \frac{my_2+ny_1}{m+n}\right).

Length of AB. d = \sqrt{(6-2)^2 + (7-3)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 16} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2} \approx 5.66 units.

Midpoint of AB. \left(\frac{2+6}{2}, \frac{3+7}{2}\right) = (4, 5).

Point dividing AB in the ratio 1:3. With m = 1, n = 3: x = \frac{1(6) + 3(2)}{4} = \frac{12}{4} = 3 and y = \frac{1(7) + 3(3)}{4} = \frac{16}{4} = 4. The point is (3, 4).

Area of triangle ABC. \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}\left|x_1(y_2-y_3) + x_2(y_3-y_1) + x_3(y_1-y_2)\right|.

= \frac{1}{2}\left|2(7-3) + 6(3-3) + 8(3-7)\right| = \frac{1}{2}\left|8 + 0 - 32\right| = \frac{1}{2}(24) = 12 square units.

Check by base and height. Side AC is horizontal with length 8 - 2 = 6. The height from B is 7 - 3 = 4. Area = \frac{1}{2}\times 6\times 4 = 12. This agrees.

Quantity Result
Length AB 4\sqrt2 units
Midpoint of AB (4, 5)
Point dividing AB as 1:3 (3, 4)
Area of the triangle 12 square units

Conclusion. A single set of formulas gives every length, point and area, and a second method confirms the area.

Model answer D3: arithmetic sequence (10 marks)

Introduction. A sequence in which each term is obtained by adding the same number to the previous term is called an arithmetic sequence. The fixed number is the common difference d.

The general term is t_n = a + (n-1)d and the sum of n terms is S_n = \frac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right].

General term. Here a = 3 and d = 7 - 3 = 4 (also 11 - 7 = 4 and 15 - 11 = 4). So t_n = 3 + (n-1)4 = 4n - 1.

Test. t_1 = 3, t_2 = 7, t_3 = 11, t_4 = 15, which agree with the given terms.

20th term. t_{20} = 4(20) - 1 = 79.

Sum of 20 terms. S_{20} = \frac{20}{2}\left[2(3) + 19(4)\right] = 10\,(6 + 76) = 10\times 82 = 820. Check with the average method: \frac{3 + 79}{2}\times 20 = 41\times 20 = 820.

Is 99 a term? Put 4n - 1 = 99, so 4n = 100 and n = 25, a whole number. Hence 99 is the 25th term. For comparison, 100 is not a term because 4n = 101 gives a fraction.

Question Working Answer
General term 3 + (n − 1)4 4n − 1
20th term 4(20) − 1 79
Sum of 20 terms 10(6 + 76) 820
Is 99 a term? 4n − 1 = 99 Yes, n = 25

Conclusion. Once a and d are known, every question on an arithmetic sequence reduces to substitution in two formulas, and a term is checked by solving for n.

Chapter summary

  • A 2-mark answer is two visible steps; a 4-mark answer is figure or table, formula, substitution, working and a checked answer.
  • Relations and functions: list ordered pairs, then read domain, range and inverse; a function needs exactly one image for every member of the domain.
  • Polynomials and sequences: collect like terms; check products by substituting a number; find t_n by differences, then test it on every given term.
  • Limit: substitute, or factorise and cancel a \frac{0}{0} form; compare the left-hand and right-hand values.
  • Matrix: same order to add or subtract; solve X+A=B as X=B-A; add two matrix equations to find X and Y.
  • Coordinate geometry: compare squared lengths; use the section formula for trisection and quarter points; area by formula or the arrow method.
  • Trigonometry: draw the right triangle, name p, b, h, choose the ratio; prove identities from one side.
  • Vector and transformation: head minus tail; parallel by x_1y_2=x_2y_1; undo a transformation with its inverse.
  • Statistics: tables for \sum fx and \sum fm; order the data for medians and quartiles; use the modal-class formula for grouped data.
